segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then I heard a loud voice from the sanctuary saying to the seven angels,

segments.speaker: God
segments.text: “Go and pour out the seven bowls of the fury of God on the earth.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So the first went and poured out his bowl on the earth, and foul and painful sores broke out on the people who had the mark of the beast and who worshiped its image.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The second poured out his bowl into the sea, and it became blood like that of a dead person, and every living creature died, all that were in the sea.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The third poured out his bowl into the rivers and the springs of water, and they became blood.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I heard the angel of the waters saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You are just, you who are and who were, the Holy One, because you have passed these judgments,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: for they poured out the blood of holy ones and prophets, and you have given them blood to drink. They deserve it.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I heard the altar saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Yes, Lord God the Almighty, true and just are your judgments.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The fourth poured out his bowl on the sun, and it was allowed to scorch people with fire.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: People were scorched with great heat, and they blasphemed the name of God, who has authority over these plagues, and they did not turn back to give him glory.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The fifth poured out his bowl on the throne of the beast, and its kingdom was plunged into darkness. People gnawed their tongues because of the pain,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and they blasphemed the God of heaven because of their pains and their sores, and they did not turn back from their deeds.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The sixth poured out his bowl on the great river, the Euphrates, and its water was dried up, so that the way might be prepared for the kings from the rising of the sun.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I saw, coming out of the mouth of the dragon and out of the mouth of the beast and out of the mouth of the false prophet, three unclean spirits like frogs;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for they are spirits of demons performing signs, which go out to the kings of the whole inhabited world to gather them for the battle of the great day of God the Almighty.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Look, I am coming like a thief. Blessed is the one who stays awake and keeps his clothes on, so that he will not walk around naked and people see his shame.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they gathered them to the place that is called in Hebrew Armageddon.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The seventh poured out his bowl on the air, and a loud voice came out of the sanctuary, from the throne, saying,

segments.speaker: God
segments.text: “It is done!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And there were flashes of lightning, rumblings, and peals of thunder, and there was a great earthquake, such as had not happened since people came to be on the earth, so mighty an earthquake, so great.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The great city split into three parts, and the cities of the nations fell. And Babylon the great was remembered before God, to be given the cup of the wine of the fury of his wrath.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Every island fled, and no mountains were to be found.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And great hailstones, about a talent in weight, came down from the sky on people; and people blasphemed God because of the plague of hail, for that plague was exceedingly great.

notes.note: Greek has two words that English Bibles usually both render “temple”: one for the whole complex with its courts, and this one for the building where God dwells. Here it is the heavenly sanctuary that 15:8 has just described as filled with smoke. Most English versions have “temple”.

The Greek word names hot, passionate anger. A different word, the usual one for “wrath”, stands beside it in verse 19 (“the fury of his wrath”). Most versions have “wrath” here, though several use “fury” or “fierceness” in verse 19; “fury” is used throughout this chapter to keep the two words distinct.

The speaker is not identified. Because 15:8 says no one could enter the sanctuary until the seven plagues were finished, most interpreters take this to be God’s own voice, as in verse 17, where the voice comes “from the throne”. The voice does speak of God in the third person, and some take it to be an angel’s.

Greek has a single word-family where English has two (righteous/just, righteousness/justice). Because the subject here and in verse 7 is God’s judging, “just” is used. The King James Version has “righteous”, and most modern versions have “just”.

The King James Version reads “which art, and wast, and shalt be”. That wording comes from a reading introduced into sixteenth-century printed editions and has no known Greek manuscript support. The manuscripts read “the Holy One”, and modern editions and translations follow them.

The traditional “saints” now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue. The Greek word is used of all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint’s language for Israel. Many translations keep “saints”, and others use “God’s people”.

“Repent” now centers on feeling sorry. The Greek verb carries the prophets’ call to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct. Most translations keep “repent” as an established term that readers understand to include a change of life.

The Euphrates was the ideal eastern boundary of the land promised to Israel, and in the first century it was the frontier between the Roman world and the Parthian empire, the power Rome feared most. The drying up of waters to open a way echoes the exodus and the crossing of the Jordan, and the prophets speak of God drying up rivers in connection with Babylon’s fall (for example, Isaiah 44:27).

notes.phrase: I am coming like a thief
notes.note: The narrative is interrupted by an unannounced first-person saying. Its content matches the words of the risen Jesus earlier in the book (3:3) and his sayings about the thief in the Gospels, so it is taken as his voice. Many versions set the verse in parentheses.

The Greek verb is singular. A neuter plural subject regularly takes a singular verb, so the subject is most naturally the three spirits of verse 14, hence “they gathered”. It could also be read as “he gathered”, with God as the subject; the King James Version has “he”.

The Greek spelling is closer to “Harmagedon”; the familiar English form is kept here. The name is usually explained as Hebrew for “mountain of Megiddo”, after the site of famous Old Testament battles (Judges 5:19; 2 Kings 23:29). Megiddo lies on a plain, not a mountain, and the derivation remains disputed.

A talent was the largest common unit of weight. Its value varied by standard and period, from roughly sixty to ninety pounds or more (about twenty-six to forty kilograms). Many modern versions give “about a hundred pounds”.

candidates.reason: It recurs through Revelation alongside ὀργή and in the phrase “the fury of his wrath”, and versions waver between wrath, fury, anger and passion; the two words need fixed, distinct renderings.
The word means “blow” or “wound” as well as “plague”, and it runs through Revelation 9–22 as a linked series that should read consistently.
It is distinct from κόσμος and γῆ and is sometimes used of the Roman empire (Luke 2:1); versions flatten it to “world” or “earth” inconsistently.
It is a different word from ἅγιος, with a sense of devout or faithful, yet both are usually rendered “holy”; a decision is needed on whether to distinguish them.
Versions alternate between “war” and “battle” across Revelation (12:7; 16:14; 19:19; 20:8), and the linked passages should match.
